Sir THOMAS WHITE (Minister of Finance) moved that the House do to-morrow go into committee on the following proposed resolutions:
Resolved, that it is expedient to authorize the payment out of the Consolidated Revenue Fund of a bounty of two cents per pound on zinc or spelter, containing not more than two per cent of impurities, produced in Canada from zino ores mined in Canada; provided the standard price of zinc or spelter in London, England, at the time of production is less than £38.19.3 sterling per ton of two thousand two hundred and forty (2.240) pounds, when the bounty payable shall be an amount equal to the difference between such standard prices per ton and £36.19.3 per ton. Further provided, that in no event shall bounty be payable when the price received for zinc or spelter by the producer is 8 cents or more per pound, and that no bounty shall be payable on zinc or spelter to the producer during the continuation of the war, and in no event on zinc or spelter produced after July 31, 1917.

Whilst I do not object to the censoring of foreign letters, and agree that it is necessary during rvar time, I must enter a most emphatic protest against the opening of letters addressed to me at my residence in Ottawa from points in Canada. For the third time since last summer letters addressed from Montreal to Ottawa have been censored. I quite understand that letters coming, for instance, from the United States or from Europe might be censored, tout I think, that my hon. friend should instruct his officers in Montreal not to open domestic leters. He should appoint men of intelligence who would not be so impertinent as to open letters written from points in Canada.
I think my hon. friend is perfectly right. The opening of his letters must have been the result of some stupid blunder. Instructions will be given to see that nothing of that kind occurs again.

I was just about to rise to make the same complaint. I received, a letter to-day from Montreal, censored. I think I am well enough known for my Canadian correspondence to be free from suspicion. If my correspondence were coming from a foreign country, perhaps some over-zealous official might think it treasonable; but the censoring of mail coming from Montreal, I think, is more stupid than anything else. Hon. C. J. DOHERTY (Minister of Justice) moved the second reading of Bill No. 86, to amend the Prisons and Reformatories Act.
What is this Bill about?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
As I explained when the Bill was introduced, certain establishments designed as industrial farms have been established by the Ontario Government for the reception of prisoners sentenced to a term of imprisonment shorter than a penitentiary sentence. Under present conditions the Ontario Reformatory, and, I think, one other institution come under the provisions of the Prisons and Reformatories Act. One purpose of this Bill is to extend those provisions so as to make them applicable to the other institutions known as industrial farms. Besides the one attached to the reformatory at Guelph, there is one at Toronto, which is about completed; one at Fort William, and one at Burwash. In addition to making certain sections applicable to these institutions, there are sections giving power to the provincial authorities to transfer from the* common jails to the reformatory, or to the industrial farms, prisoners sentenced to the common jail, and, where conditions render that course necessary, or desirable, to order their return to the common jail.
There are sections also specifically making the dispositions in the first section of the Act, with regard to prisons for male prisoners, applicable to similar institutions established for female prisoners. There is a further provision conferring upon what is known in Ontario as the parole board powers to be exercised in dealing with prisoners who have been sentenced to indeter minate sentences; that it to say, prisoners upon whom the courts, under the provisions of the law, have imposed a sentence of, say, not less than three months, of of not more than twenty-four months. The parole hoardi is a body constituted by the Lieutenant Governor, and has been in existence for some years. It is now charged

with looking into the cases of different prisoners, and at present make recommendations to the Department of'Justice looking to their release. This confers upon them powers to deal with prisoners, during that period of the sentence which is indeterminate, in the way of allowing them to he released from close custody under obligation to report, and under surveillance, subject to conditions which shall toe approved by the Minister of Justice. It further confers upon them a power, after the terms and conditions in regard to any such prisoner have been complied with, to report to the Minister of Justice recommending liberation. These different dispositions are considered of importance by the provincial authorities for the purpose o>f carrying out more effectively their views with regard to the reformation of prisoners. It has seemed to us that these provisions asked for, would undoubtedly have that result, and should be encouraged to enable the system tO' be carried out under the best possible conditions. Personally, I am disposed to think that the hopes of the Ontario authorities with regard to its success will be fulfilled. In any event, under these provisions there will be opportunity to give the system a full and a fair trial.
Hon. GEORGE P. GRAHAM: This action of the Minister of Justice is in line with the view that I have entertained for a good many years. From remarks that I have had occasion to make on the question of capital punishment, the minister knows that my views arc strongly along the line that there is something in nearly every human being to reform, if we can get at it, and that every opportunity ought to be given to develop that which is best in the individual who has been convicted of a crime of greater or less magnitude. The object of punishment for crime committed is not primarily to get even, if I might put it in ordinary parlance, with the man who [DOT]has committed a crime; nor is it one of revenge. The great object of punishment is the protection of society in order that the crime committed by the individual may not be repeated by some other individual. That is, I believe, the prime cause of action against men who have committed crimes. But there is a second object, or there ought to be, and that is the reformation of the individual who lias committed the crime, perhaps under some great stress, perhaps under mental pressure of which even the 
courts know nothing or are unable to ascertain in the strictest trial. Holding that view, I have always maintained, as the minister knows, that capital punishment ought to be abolished, and that society would be protected just as well toy imprisonment for life, while the opportunity would toe afforded to the criminal to reform.
This Bill is along these lines, although it applies to those who have been convicted of crimes not of a capital nature. For a time, a 6hort time I admit, the central prison in Toronto was under the department over which I presided in the Provincial Government, and one of the things that struck me during the first few weeks of my tenure of office was the absolute impropriety of confining in a prison all prisoners who had been convicted to serve a term of less than two years without giving .them any opportunity for reformation during that period. The crimes were trivial perhaps, (and without reflecting upon the bench at all, we know that its occupants have livers, and that -sometimes they do not work in the same sympathetic way as they do at other times, so that a man or a woman convicted of a comparatively trivial offence will get a term of two years less than one day, which seems extreme at times. There is no doubt that in that individual there is something good which, if appealed to in the proper way, would develop in such an manner that the punishment might be cut in half, or even further reduced. In committing these smaller offences particularly, the individual is often moved by a momentary impulse, and there is nothing radically criminal in his or her make-up. But if that individual is confined, and deprived of the opportunity of mingling in ' a measure with the outside world, and of retaining his manhood or her womanhood, my view is that they become worse instead of better, anid that punishment becomes a deterrent of good citizenship rather than an encouragement of it.
The Central prison in Toronto is in the heart of the city, in a district which was not always -so populous as now, but in the midst of the hum of a great thriving ei-tv like Toronto is no place for a central prison. The taking of -these prisoners out of that institution; the -passing of this law; the action o-f the Ontario Legislature in establishing industrial farms; the giving of an opportunity to the prisoner to get out into the open air

because his surroundings have a great deal to do with the working of a prisoner's mind-all this is a step in the

right direction, and I believe that we shall do a great deal more in this direction during the next few years than we have done in the past.
I have always taken a deep interest in this particular phase of our public policy and have at times perhaps been considered meddlesome and somewhat of a nuisance. I have even been accused of interfering with the course of justice; but the hon. minister can understand the viewpoint from which I look at these matters. My conduct has never been impelled by the desire to interfere with the law, but I have always held strenuously to the idea that we ought to treat these unfortunate people in the most humane manner possible and give them every opportunity to return again to good citizenship. I have experienced the difficulty, particularly in respect to boys sent to the reformatory, that the police magistrate and the chief of police find it very difficult to get themselves into a frame of mind to assist in securing the release on parole of a boy whom they have sent to the reformatory. Thy seem to hesitate, considering it as a reflection on their judgment. In making my appeals to them, I have never looked at the matter in tjiat light. I have argued with them that they were not casting any reflection upon their own judgment or conduct by lending a little aid, if necessary, to get a young person out of the reformatory. This legislation will, I think, be in a measure a hint to some that Governments are beginning to look on the law and its execution from a different angle; that one of the chief objects is the reformation of the individual in conjunction with the protection of society. I have not carefully considered the details of the Bill, but I understand that the principle is as I have stated, and that it goes a little further and allows a person convicted an opportunity to make good under the new privileges, and that if the individual does make good, he or she will have an opportunity to be restored to society in a much shorter time than under the old conditions.

I would like to say a word or two in support of this legislation. Like the hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. 'Graham), I believe this is simply pioneer legislation, and that before very long we shall have much more legislation of this character on the statute books, because most people to-day realize that prison life, just as every other kind of life, is going
through a process of evolution. This Bill has been foreshadowed for some time.
As the hon. member for South Renfrew has said, the Central Prison, which is the jail or penitentiary for the province of Ontario, was situated, and what is left of it is still (Situated, in a very populous part of the city of Toronto. It has now been removed to Guelph, where there is a splendid institution, to study which those who are interested in the reformation of mankind and in prison reform have sent delegates from all parts of the States. It is regarded as a model institution designed to assist in the reform of unfortunate criminals, and it is doing magnificent work.
In 1914 the legislature of Ontario, realizing the good work that is being done by the Industrial Farm at-Guelph, and feeling that wider legislation is required along that line, passed an Act respecting industrial farms, empowering any city or county to establish, in lieu of the old common jail for its locality, an industrial farm, to which the prisoners would be transferred from the common jail and treated in a manner better calculated to incite them to mend their ways	and to begin
the leading of a better life. The common jail of the county	of York was
like the Central prison, in a thickly populated part of the city of Toronto and some four or five hundred prisoners were kept there; it was not desirable either for the prisoners or for the community that they Should be there. Acting upon that legislation, the city of Toronto has spent about $450,000 in buying land a few miles from Toronto where they have established the Hill Crest farm, on which they are now treating a large number of prisoners on the prison reform basis. The prisoners are there given a chance to breathe the fresh air, to begin life anew; every opportunity is afforded to them to become good citizens again. Although the Central prison in Toronto wsa an immense place surrounded by an 'almost unsealea'ble wall, the record is that fewer prisoners have escaped from Guelph where they are at liberty to run away than used to escape over the high walls of the Central prison, which proves that if men are treated humanely, they are satisfied to serve their prison term, and prompted to endeavour to lead honourable lives. Up to the present, the difficulty in dealing with offences under the Criminal Code-and most offences for which men are committed to jail are code offiences-has been that the committing magistrate or

judge has power to send convicted prisoners only to the common jail of the county where the offence is committed or any other common jail that he may designate, there being no provision (until this legislation is passed to commit prisoners or convicts to any industrial or prison farm. It is because of that difficulty that this legislation has been introduced. The province of Ontario, having first established a large farm at Guelph, has now established two prison farms, one at Sudbury and the other at Fort William, in one of which an entire township is occupied, where the prisoners breathe an atmosphere of liberty and are given an opportunity to again become good members of society.
This amendment applies to both males and females; it includes those who may be transferred from the Mercer reformatory to an industrial farm, and the industrial farm now established in connection with the common jail of the county of York has ample accommodation for both male and female prisoners. If this amendment is passed, it will offer, inducements to and encourage other 'counties, municipalities, and cities, not only throughout Ontario, but in the other provinces of the Dominion, to establish industrial farms, which will mean a real and substantial reform in the treatment of prisoners. I commend the legislation in every way to the members of 'the House.

I would crave the indulgence of the House for a' moment to draw the attention of the Minister of Justice to a case which has come to my notice, of a person convicted of a criminal offence in western Ontario. Under the law applying to the case, this person was sentenced in open court, in the presence of his mother, a coterie of his friends, and the public, to a period of one year. The prisoner was sent to the place of incarceration, where by good conduct, splendid deportment, obedience to the rules and regulations, he hoped to be accorded the usual allowance off his sentence for good conduct. His good conduct entirely justified him in making that request, but when he made it, to his pain and mortification, it turned out, that although the sentence pronounced in open court in the presence of the public had been imprisonment for one year, he was still subject to a further year by way of indeterminate sentence, although the judge had pronounced nothing of the kind in open court.

Does the Minister of
Justice agree with that interpretation of the law.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I do not think it is a correct interpretation of the law. In one or two instances I understand the law providing for indeterminate sentences has been interpreted in that sense, and it has certainly been a matter of surprise to me.
Mir. iPUGSLHY:	To me too. I never
heard of such a thing.

I had never heard of it before, and that is why I am bringing the matter before the House, so that the case may go 'on Hansard for the consideration of those who are charged with the administration of criminal justice, and in order that such an abuse may not	occur in the	future.	In all
fairness to the prisoner and the the public at large, I think that a judge when sentencing a prisoner convicted of an indictable offence, should be compelled to state the length of the sentence. It is absolutely unfair that a prisoner should be sent to a prison under the idea that he has to serve only one year, and then for him to find that not only has he not the opportunity of getting the sentence reduced by good conduct, but that owing to a peculiar interpretation of the law, he has to serve a further period of one year. I agree with the remarks of the hon member for South Renfrew as to the object of punishment. But this was a case of a young man taking his first false step, and after fulfilling the sentence pronounced by the judge, he found that the sentence had been doubled. I- do not think that kind of administration of justice,-I would rather call it administration of injustice-which puts the iron into the soul of a young man who has committed his first offence, will meet with the approval of the people of this country. I think it will have the effect of bringing the administration of justice into contempt, and of making a rebel against society out of a man who, although perhaps feeling that he deserves to be convicted, at the same time feels that he is being unjustly treated by having to serve two years when the judge only sentenced him for one.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
One word with regard
to the particular case that has been mentioned. I said that I had heard that there had been such an interpretation .put upon the law. I may say that the particular case '

to which the hon. member refers came before us upon an application for release, but on the face of the documents sent to us it appeared that the judge had sentenced this young man to not less than one year, and not more than two, and of course the documents before us were all that we had to go' upon as to what the sentence actually was. It was represented in another case that the sentence had only been for a period less than two years, but there again we made inquiry of the court, and were assured that the sentence as returned to us was the sentence that had been pronounced. I confess, and perhaps it may be of some usefulness that I should say so, that I cannot possibly follow the interpretation put upon the section, which implies that the mere fact of a judge imposing one definite period necessarily carries with it a further indefinite period. As I understand it, the only section which empowers the imposition of these indeterminate sentences is section 44 of the Act that is now sought to be amended, and to my mind it is perfectly 'dear that it merely confers upon the judge the power of sentencing a man to a reformatory for a term of not less than three months', and for an indeterminate period thereafter of not more than two years. How it is inferred from that that if the judge did impose a definite sentence and added nothing more, that the balance of two years should automatically attach to the definite period pronounced, I confess I am unable to comprehend.

I presume the reason the prison farm was started at Guelph by the Ontario Government was because it had come to the conclusion that there was1 something in -a man, even if the law regarded him as a criminal, to which one might appeal for his own good. I think the farm has done a great deal of good, and I believe that this Act is also in the right direction. I must confess that a convicted criminal has my warm sympathy. I havie no maudlin sentiment for a man who commits an offence against the law; hp must be taught that he cannot violate the law without being punished; but I do think that more good could be accomplished by humane treatment, by appealing to the better side of a man's nature, than by confining him within four walls, and obliging him to consort with old and hardened criminals. There are reasons why we should have a great deal of consideration for the young fellow who has committed his first offence, and,
first of all, because under the laws as they exist to-day, a money value is placed upon crime. For instance, two men may commit the same offence. One of them, a rich man, imbibes too freely, becomes disorderly, and is run in by the police. Next morning the magistrate gives him the choice of paying $10 or going for thirty days, and having the $10 he pays it and goes home. Another fellow commits exactly the same offence, and is run in by the police. He comes before the magistrate, and is given the option of paying $10 or going up for thirty days. He has not got the money, and he goes up for thirty days. In other words, the law tells the man: You may become drunk and disorderly if you have enough to pay for it; and if you put up a sufficient amount of cash we will let it go at that; but if you have not the necessary amount of cash, we will consider your lack of cash to be represented by so many days in jail. That, on the face o.f it, seems to me a little unfair; and that is one reason why I think that some consideration should be given especially to the young fellows. What I wish particularly to say is, that if it is right-and I have not heard anybody dispute its wisdom-to establish the prison farm at Guelph with its mode of treatment of criminals, that policy ought to be extended to apply particularly to the young men who are first offenders and who are sentenced to longer terms than two years. This Bill applies only to the men who are sentenced for a period of two years or more. I hope to see the day when the boys and young men of from 17 to. 20 years of age, now sent to the penitentiary, will be given a chance such as these prisoners are given who are sent to the prison farm at Guelph. I honestly think that, under existing conditions, we legislators are committing far greater crimes in sending the boys to the penitentiary and obliging them to put in years at no other employment than breaking stone, than any that the boys or youths committed that caused them to be sent to the penitentiary. . I hope that1 this Bill, which is in the right direction, will, in the course of time, be extended, or that the policy that it embodies will be extended, to apply to the younger prisoners who are sentenced for the first time to the penitentiary, and so give them a chance to recover their manhood and become again good and useful citizens.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the . second time, and the House went into Committee thereon, Mr. Rhodes in the Chair.
On section 1-Prisoners may be sentenced to Industrial Farm, etc:

I am very greatly impressed with what my hon. friend from Frontenac (Mr. Edwards) has said. It appears that, while this .Bill iis in the right direction, it is desira'ble that similar provision should be made with reference to prisoners who may be confined in the penitentiary. It often happens that judges sentence boys to the penitentiary whom other judges would have sent to the jail. It does seem to me, instead of allowing the reform of the penitentiaries to stand until some distant time,, that now, when we are dealing with this question, is the time to provide for those prisoners sentenced to the penitentiary as well as for those who are provided for in the Bill. I would suggest to the Minister of Justice that, having heard the expression of opinion by hon. members of the House, he should consider whether he might not take a little time and try to extend the provisions of this Bill so as to give a discretion to the minister, or to his officials, to exercise some clemency in respect of persons who may be confined in' the penitentiary. I think it most unfortunate that young lads who have not been guilty of any previous offence, and whose character is in the formative stage, should be kept confined in the penitentiary, there to mingle with hardened criminals and so have their lives practically destroyed. I do not see why a move in the same direction might not be made with regard to prisoners confined in the penitentiary, allowing the Department of Justice tp make arrangements with the provinces, by means of which the prisoners might be sent to the industrial farms and treated the same as the other prisoners there. I think this Bill is a move in the right direction, but we ought not to stop here, but should go further and act upon the suggestion which has been made.

I desire to add one word in corroboration, of what the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley) has said. In the course of the prison investigation it was brought out that a boy of 16 or 17, whose name I have forgotten, had been sentenced by a magistrate, from the county of Hastings, I think, to a term of four or five years in the penitentiary. His offence was the stealing from the farmer with whom he was employed of an old silver watch and about two dollars and a half in money. The magistrate thought that in the penitentiary he might learn a trade. Probably the magis-

trate's intention was good. But the boy was sent to work on the stone pile alongside of old criminals, some of whom had been in prison for years. It was impressed on my mind, as I think it must have been impressed on the mind of every person who read the evidence, that here was a miscarriage of justice and a decided wrong.
Would the hon. member state how long ago that was.

His term must be very nearly up now. It seemed to me that the last chance that boy had of be-4 p.m. coming a good and useful citizen was taken away from him when he was sentenced to four years at labour of that kind. This is an illustration of a decidedly wrong method, one that it is our bounden duty to change at the earliest opportunity.
I would call the attention of the hon. member to the fact that evidently this case was adjudicated upon before the passage of the Industrial Farms Act.
Very likely.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
There is no doubt that it would be desirable that in the penitentiaries, as far as possible, we should arrive at a method of getting.young prisoners separated from older and more hardened offenders.
As to the sentence that has just been referred to, that, of course, is a matter which is in the hands of the judge. If the sentence was too long or too heavy- and upon the statement of fact's as made by the hon. member it would look as if it were-that shows a lack of judgment on the part of the magistrate who pronounced it. As to the suggestion of the hon. member for St. John that we should amend this Bill with a view to doing something with regard to penitentiaries, I would point out that an amendment' in that line would hardly be relevant to the subject matter of this Bill. Whether we ought to take action in that regard is another question, but' we are now dealing with the institutions under the control of the provincial authorities. Improvement in penitentiaries necessitating legislation would form, I think, the proper subject matter of an amendment to the Penitentiaries Act. It does happen from time to time that" young boys are sentenced to a penitentiary where it would be better to sentence them to other institutions, but we, of course, have to receive into the penitentiaries those who are sentenced

to them. I do believe that if we could bring about a system under which our prisoners could be separated into classes, it would be a great advantage. The question has had much consideration and examination, and it seems to me that practically th' only effective way of doing that would be to establish separate institutions. The dividing up of prisoners within the same institution is attended with very great difficulty. Of course, the providing of separate institutions for different classes of prisoners would involve our undertaking the establishing of new institutions. I hope that it may not be very long before we shall be able to do that, but the present time does not seem to be the most propitious for the undertaking of large expenditures in.that direction. In the meantime we do endeavour as far as possible to protect the youthful prisoner. In the exercise of clemency the youth of the prisoner and the fact of its being his first offence is always given the most serious consideration. As to the case referred to, I have not the exact facts at the moment, and therefore I am not in a position to speak particularly with regard to it. Section 1 of this Bill applies sections 18 to 20 of the Prisons and Reformatories Act to the industrial farms. Under the law as it now stands, these provisions are applicable to the Ontario reformatory and to the Mercer reformatory. The substance of the sections of the present Act is that any judge sentencing a prisoner to any of these institutions may sentence such prisoner for a term not more than one-sixth longer than the term at present prescribed by law for the offence, and any such sentence may be carried out in such prison, although it is for any term not exceeding two years and four months. The next section establishes in these prisons a system a remission analogous to that which exists in the penitentiaries, providing that the prisoner may by good conduct and industry earn five days per month. There is a sliding scale which runs up as high as ten days per month. The third section provides that breach of the prison laws and regulations may entail deprivation of this remission. The whole effect of the first section of this Bill is to make these three sections, which are already applicable to the reformatory institutions that I have mentioned, applicable to the industrial farms that have been and are being established.

Section agreed to.
On section 2-Board of Parole:

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The Lieutenant Governor in Council of Ontario has, under legislation enacted by that province, appointed what is called a Board of Parole. Under this legislation, the Board of Parole has power to look into the cases of persons imprisoned for violation of provincial law. The legislature could not, of course, deal with the cases of persons condemned under the Dominion law. The purpose of this section is to give to this Parole Board, in cases where persons are sentenced for indeterminate periods-as, for instance, under the section to which I referred a few minutes ago, where a person may be sentenced to any of these reformatory institutions for a period of not less than three months and not more than twenty-four months-the power of releasing the prisoner from close confinement upon conditions to be laid down and submitted to and approved by the Minister of Justice. It goes on further to provide that in such cases, where the conditions have been complied with by the prisoner, this Parole Board may recommend a prisoner for final discharge. It was not necessary, perhaps, to confer tnat last power by statute, but its being put in the statute gives the recommendation of the board an official status. I may say that such recommendation on the part of the Parole Board would almost invariably be followed.

Section agreed to.
Bill reported, read the third time, and passed.

Is it considered necessary now to have all these subsidies for this traffic? Would not the traffic pay for the services without subsidies?

speakeroldname: Sir GEORGE FOSTER (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speechtext:
Whilst on general principles it may be thought that these subsidies are not necessary, and that with the building of railways they ought to be done away with, yet, taking this service, fo.r instance, it is a service which is not provided for by railways in any way. It is a coast service running from Halifax westerly, and doing work which has to be done by vessels and which cannot be done in any other way.

There is quite an amount of traffic. It is not like an Atlantic or a Pacific service in amount, but it is equally important to the people who are served by it as the larger services are to the larger scope of trade and traffic which is served by them. Last year, on this service, there were carried 4,820 tons of freight. The amount of subsidy earned and paid was $3,000. This is a trip subsidy, and if trips are omitted they are not paid for, so isometimes a less total sum will be paid than is provided for by the subsidy.

I was not objecting to
that particular item, but I wanted the information.

Most of these
coast services are of that class.

Inquiry arose in the
House the other evening, when the Estimates of the Postmaster General were going through, as-to the basis on which these subventions were given, and as to the cost of carrying the mail, and the number of steamship companies that were being paid for carrying the mail. The Postmaster General very correctly replied that that was very largely in the Department of Trade and Commerce Would the minister tell us just the basis on which the mails are carried?

These services, what we call local services, are not primar

 ily mail services, but every one of them is under contract to carry whatever mails may be placed on board, and quite a number of them do carry mails. The larger ocean services, such as those on the Pacific from Vancouver and Victoria to the Far East, are steamship subsidies, and come under my department. We take the vote and we pay the cost of such a service. We carry the mails, and the Postmaster General has the arrangement of the mails and sees that they are despatched. There is no accounting from the Post Office Department to the Department of Trade and Commerce for mail carriage; it is a subvention which covers both the trade and the mails. Properly, I think, although the present system has prevailed from the time this service was inaugurated, there ought to be an accounting between the two departments so that we would know exactly the value of a service like that for mail purposes and its value for commercial purposes. That, however, in the inception was not adopted as a policy, and has not

been since. Exactly similar to that is the Atlantic mail service, where the Department of Trade and Commerce pays the subsidy and the steamships are obliged to carry the mail for that subsidy, and in that respect likewise there is no accounting 'between the two departments. Some time or other, when this war is over, I hope these two departments will get together and establish an atocounting system between them. It is obviously just that this 'should be done. The Post Office Department is supposed to carry the mails of the country. It gets the revenue and shows its accounts, 'but the Department of Trade and Commerce, on these two important routes, we will say, carries the mails and pays for them. That is, the country does not know exactly w'hat the cost of carrying its mail is. However, from the inception of this service many many years ago until the present time, that is the system which has been pursued.

How many steamship
lines really do carry the mails on the Pacific and on the Atlantic?
It was slow.

It was slow, but sometimes mail packages went by that route, and the service has been so much interrupted since the war that it has not amounted to very much.
Mail Subsidies and Steamship Subventions- local services-steam service between Halifax and Spry bay and ports in Cape Breton, $4,000.

Is that the. service that called at Port Felix last year?
\

This is the service Which serves the southeastern coast of Nova Scotia. It runs from Halifax, and touches, or did touch, at the point mentioned by my hon. friend, and then goes on to the Cape Breton ports.
Will the minister give the names of the different ports touched at?

Halifax, Jeddore, Owl's Head, Tangier, Pope's Harbour, Ship Harbour, Sheet Harbour, Sober Island, Spry Bay, St. Peter's, Arichat, West Arichat, Poulamon and L'Archeveque. The minister has the general power of adding ports at which the vessels under this contract shall stop, but he has to be pretty cautious and reasonable in exercising that power, because he might ask them to stop at more places than the steamship owners had contemplated. when the subsidy was granted.
Has the contract been signed for the current year?
It has been signed by the steamship company, and will be signed by me, and then I will take up with the company the question of adding one or two ports and try to do what I reasonably can.

If the minister will look at the list of ports he has read he will find that the first five or six are all in Halifax county. Then it jumps the whole of Guys-borough county, a distance of over 100 miles, without providing for a call until the vessels get to Cape Breton. It seems to ignore quite a long stretch of the coast where communication is very necessary. Last year, or the year before last, an arrangement was imade between the merchants of Port Felix and the owners of the ship to call at that point, which is in Tor bay. It is a village at which a somewhat thriving fish business is carried on, and it has no communication whatever except by that boat. The merchants, who were attempting to develop a fresh fish trade by sending their fish to Mulgrave and Halifax for sale, will be badly hit if they have no communication whatever. I have heard from them by letter and by telegraph, and there is quite a little excitement down there over the question. The owners, I believe, threatened to withdraw the ship for the present season unless, they obtained a larger subsidy. I understand that the subsidy amounts to $4,000, but if the minister has the power to add an additional port I would like very much if he would exercise
it, because it means that these merchants will have to give up business altogether if they fail to obtain communication. Their only alternative would be to salt their fish, or cure them in some other way, and that is not as profitable as sending them forward fresh.
How far is it across from Port Felix to Queensport?

Probably eight or ten miles, but it is a rather mountainous country, with a very bad road, and it would be altogether out of the question to take the fish that way. It will be very inconvenient to those people if no steamboat calls. I know the minister will do all he can, but I call his attention to the fact that the county of Halifax is rather generously treated, there being calls at five or six different ports, while, for over 100 miles along the coast no call is made at all. He will see that it is unusual for such a long distance to be ignored. Some of the ports in Halifax county are very small, and I question whether they have anything like the business that is done at Port Felix. I hope the minister will take the matter up, and, if possible, arrange for a call to be made at that point.

When the subsidy was first granted this was exclusively a Halifax county service, and, for a good many years, it went no further than Spry Bay. Two years ago, however, I think it was extended in order to assist the Cape Breton ports, so that, actually, it was a Halifax county service which was extended for the benefit of my hon. friend's county.
The subsidy was increased.

Maybe it was. I have already given instructions to inquire of the people of Port Felix what their marketing output would be, and also of the steamship company what they carried there last year. I have asked the supervisor of steamship companies to make a report on the matter, and when that report is received I will deal with it as well as I can.
Steam service from the opening: to the closing of navigation between Kenora and Fort Frances, $8,000.

What amount of business is done by this service? I have spent a couple of summers on the lakes and it does not seem to me there is enough business doing between Kenora and Fort Frances to justify this subsidy.
Have you a steamer for this service?

The vessel that has plied on that route for the last three or four years, an excellent vessel and giving an excellent service, has, owing to the high prices brought about by war conditions, been sold and taken off the route. I have made arrangements to have the steamer Amelia take her place. The Amelia has been plying around the shores of Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island for quite a number of years. This year she has been refitted, and if she is put into a thoroughly satisfactory condition, as they promise she will be, she will be put on that route. ,

She is a smaller and
slower vessel than the Sibyl. Will she get the full amount of the subsidy?
" Sir GEORGE FOSTER: I do not think she is as good a vessel as the Sibyl, but when the improvements have been made she will be a very eligible vessel. I sent advertisements to twenty-seven different companies, but got no answer from any of them with the single exception of the Amelia. Vessels are not to be picked up in every harbour nowadays, and it was touch and go between, getting the Amelia and having no service at all.
I think the Government purchased the Princess from the Prince Edward Island Navigation Company some years ago. She would be a very suitable boat for this service.

That vessel was intended for special service, but I had a

partial promise of the Princess from the minister in case I could get no other vessel. I had that alternative in view.
She would be much better than the Amelia for that service.
I hardly think she would, considering her draught.

The other day, when we were considering Bill No. 66, I asked if the Minister of Justice would insert a provision providing a .penalty for subsidized steamers carrying liquor in violation of the Bill we were then considering. He said the matter could be more effectively dealt with when the contract with these subsidized steamers was being entered into. I know conditions down there pretty well, and I am sure the law can be more easily evaded by steamers than by any other means. Some good might be done if the minister would draw the attention of the companies to this legislation, and to the penalties that will follow any violation of it. I fear that efforts will be made by those interested to use the steamers in violation of the law.

With reference to that, I can only say that I would consider it my duty to call the attention of any subsidized company very sharply to any yiola-tion of the law that might occur, and I do not think such a call would be disregarded. From what I know of the people connected with this boat, I have no reason to believe that any such thing .would happen.
I was not referring to this boat particularly.

My statement applies generally to all subsidized services. If they violate any of the laws of the Dominion I think they will be perfectly and thoroughly subject to discipline, and I shall have very great pleasure in calling attention to the matter.
I think the Sibyl advanced freight rates very considerably, almost doubled them, in fact.
Oh, no; a slight advance, but not very great.
Is there any provision in the contract in regard to rates?

Yes, in every contract.

Steam service between Mulgrave and Guys-borough, calling at intermediate ports, $5,500.
Has that contract been executed for the coming year?
I think so.

Are the ports of call
the same as before?

Yes.
Steam service between Pictou and Montague, calling at Murray harbour and Georgetown, $6,000.

I call the attention of
the minister to this item in connection with Bill No. 66, and state that the same remarks I made before apply to this.

Steam service between Prince Edward Island and Cape Breton and Newfoundland, $16,500.

As my hon. friend knows, the Senlac was burned and is not available for the service this year. She was probably not the best vessel that could have been obtained, but she was the only one that we could get last year, this service having been interrupted by the fact that the Dominion Coal Company's steamers did not carry on the service between Quebec and Newfoundland. I have been in communication with some parties and two vessels only have been in mind and communications are not yet carried out to the point where I would be able to say that a vessel was secured for the service, but I think the prospects are that we shall be able to obtain a vessel.

I understand that the
New York company, the owners of the steamer Florizel, which made one trip last year, I think
No.
That would be a suitable steamer for this service.
It has not been offered this year at all.
I think it could be secured.
There weie negotiations last year with reference to the Florizel, but no contract was made and no service was performed.

Steam service from the opening to the closing of navigation in 1916, between Prince Edward Island and the mainland, $12,500.

Arrangements are not entirely completed as yet, but they have gone so far that I think I can say to the committee that the service will be carried on between Sumimerside and Pointe du Chene by the Northumberland and between Charlottetown and Pictou by another vessel.
The minister has the names in the wrong order. The Northumberland plies, between Pictou and Charlottetown, and the Empress between Summer-side and Point du ChSne.
I think I am right.
This year?
Last year, too. They may change off whilst one vessel is on the slip, but the steamer Northumberland plied between Summerside and Pointe du Chene. I went over on her myself. '
It must have been for one d^iy only.	-
No. My hon. friend lives closer to the scene of action, but he is not correct.
Where does the Empress Ply?
Between Pictou and Charlottetown, part of the time at least.

It does not make any
difference, but the minister has the names the other way around.

I believe how
that my hon. friend is correct. The Empress has been disposed of and is not available for this service.
There will be no boat plying between Pictou and Charlottetown?

There will be
a boat.
What boat will that be?

I cannot say
exactly, but the service will be provided for.

The Empress is going
off the route.
So I understand.

Can the minister say,
although it is not in his department, anything in regard to the car ferry service during the corning summer?

The car ferry
service is not being carried on as such. The car ferry has been doing work between Pictou and Charlottetown, I think.

I mean for the coming
summer.

I am not able to say anything about that. All I can say is what I have said, that a service will be carried on between those two points.
Steam service between Quebec and Gaspe basin, touching at intermediate ports, $8,500.

I understand that the
steamer was lost last fall. What kind of a service have you now?

The Lady of
Gaspe was unfortunately lost. She was a very good vessel and well adapted to that traffic. Arrangements have been made this year with the owners of the Gaspesien and another vessel whose name I do not just now remember. The service will be carried on between Quebec and Gaspe basin under contract with that company.
Will the vessels call at the usual intermediate ports?
The same poTts of call as were served la6t year.

My hon. friend says that the Lady of Gaspe was an excellent boat. That is quite true, but she met with an accident on the river and was sold for scrap iion. She was repaired and is now tramping the southern seas and making something like $15,000 a month. That is the latest news I have.
Sir GEORGE FOSTER; And I suppose the saddest people on that coast are those who sold her for scrap iron.
Is the vessel obliged to come to the wharf at Mechins or does it wait in the middle of the channel to take on and land passengers or freight?

My hon. friend brought that to my attention before and I have asked for information, but it is a little difficult to get it 'because the company that owned the vessel are no longer responsible and we have not been able so far to get that information from them. I have inquired of some resident officials who may be near there. You have a customs officer at either of those places?
No.
You have a harbour master?
Yes.

He will be the man from whom we shall prolbafbly get our information as to what calls were made last year. When I get the information, I will be glad to send it to my hon. friend. The only trouble about calling at some of these places,. I believe, is lack of sufficient depth of water.
As I was the father cf this service, I may calL the service my baby.

Dangerous, in
these days-there may be an explosion.

I agree with the state-'
ment of my hon. friend from Rimouski (Mr. Boulay). As the minister is making a new arrangement with other parties to carry on the service, I hope he will see to it that the small ports get the benefit of the service. The very object of this subsidy is to secure direct communication between these ports and Quebec and Montreal. The company, of course, is always glad to stop at as few small ports as possible. The service is the fishermen's regular trade route between Matane and Gaspe and the large centres. Some years ago the fishing industry was practically stagnant in the ports of Gaspe, Rimouski and Matane, but since the establishment of this service the merchants and fishermen have benefited considerably. I hope the minister will stand by the fishermen in this eternal quarrel with the owners of the steamers. Let the steamers stop at these small ports. The service was created for that very purpose.

I desire to say a word as an addition to my former remarks, and in answer to the letter written by the owners of the steamer. They say that they could not call at Mechins on account of the lack of water. I do not know ho\v much water

their steamer draws, but there is a depth of 17 feet at low tide at Mechins wharf- that is the report I have from the people of that place. So I think it is only because they do not want to stop that they do not get to the wharf. These people are isolated from all railways, and when we pay a subvention to a company they ought to pay more attention to these ports where there is no railway than they do to other ports. As the people of that region depend on that vessel, the vessel ought to stop every time it can reach the wharf. It will not do to say, as they do in their answer, that they whistle, and, seeing nobody, they go on. If they pass at night, of course the people fcannot stay awake for the vessel, particularly when they are not advised, this being a place where there is no telegraph system. It is for the vessel to come to the wharf and not for the people to go and meet her in the middle of the channel.

The Gaspesien
draws 11 feet of water, and the Percessian 19J feet. If there is 17 feet of water at that port, the Gaspesiem would have no excuse for not calling. I have no hesitation in saying that this service, being chiefly for the small ports that have no railway communication, the companies are looked after carefully, and when we get reports that they are not calling we immediately call them to time. Sometimes we do not get a report for long afterwards.
May I refer to items that were considered while I was absent; what tenders were received for the Magdalen island service?

I stated that we had sent out twenty-seven calls for tenders, and had received only one reply, and that was on behalf of the steamer Amelia. That vessel has been accepted for the service as the only one we could get, provided that she is repaired sufficiently to do the work.

WheTe are the repairs
being made?

In Halifax,
where they do all the work for Nova Scotia.

She will receive
$18,000?

The subsidy is
$18,000; but it came to a showdown; $24,000 was asked, and at last, rather than go without a vessel, I made them an offer of $20,000. I shall ask for $2,000 more in the
Supplementary Estimates. This is one service, as my hon. friend knows, that cannot be done without.

Yes. I desire to
ask also what vessel is performing the service between Pictou, Mulgrave, and Cheti-camp?

The Kinburn,
and the contractor is Roderick 5 p.nl. McDougall, of Port Hood, N.S. Last year, they carried 315 passengers and 1,145 tons of freight, and performed 67 trips.

Is the service supposed to start from Pictou? This is a service almost as historic as the Magdalen island service, and has always been performed from the port of Pictou. But trips from Pictou of late have been very rare. What is the cause of the change? There is a great deal of traffic with northern Inverness and always has been; but there is complaint from shippers in the county that the old-time service has been lessened. What change has been made, and why?

Changes as to
ports of call?
As to time of call.

She starts from
Pictou and runs to Mulgrave. In order to make her time on the other route, and also owing to low water, bad wharves,-or no wharves, a part, of the coastline -along Nova Scotia was left out and its ports given a schooner service. The boat then goes to Mulgrave and thence north. So far as I can recollect, last year we bad very little if any complaint. I have heard from many sources that the service was satisfactory.
How often does the boat make that trip?

She makes one round trip every fortnight between Pictou and Mulgrave, calling both ways at Ari-saig, Georgeville, Cape George, Morristown, Malignant Cove, Livingstone Cove, Ballan-tyn-e Cove and Cribbin's Point. She makes two round trips each week between Mulgrave and Cheticamp, calling both ways at Port Hastings, Port Haiwkesbury, Port Hood, Port Hood Island, Margaree Harbour, Grand Etang and Eastern Harbour, and once each week at Pleasant Bay. She calls also, whenever required by the min-

ister, at Henry Island, Mabou Mouth, Inverness, Red Cape, and Port Bain.

The minister does not appreciate my point. The result of the change is, as the minister has said, that Antigonish ports have largely been left out, a coastal schooner service 'being given to the small ports. Instead of haying a weekly service from Pietou, we have a service only twice a month, and .to that extent the service has been reduced. The complaint that I have heard is that the combining of these two services would mean absolutely destroying the original trade that existed between Pietou and Antigonish and Chetieamp. The service has not been satisfactory; so far as our end of it is concerned it is impossible for one boat to make the necessary trips and give a satisfactory service.

Several considerations are involved in this. If my impression is correct, I was anxious to make the change for two reasons. One was not to have the double service if one vessel could do the whole work and the other was that the amount of traffic between Pietou and the ports beyond was comparatively small. Then again, Mulvrave and Pietou are both points on the Intercolonial and we are anxious to carry as much as possible on our road. However, I think it is true, taking the records of last year and of this year especially, that it is the general opinion that the service has been satisfactory.

Did the boat
make these trips regularly this year?
Yes.

I remind the
-.minister that I anticipated this difficulty when the change was made. I then told the hon. gentleman that one boat was not sufficient to carry on the service satisfactorily. I am not surprised that there is very little traffic between Pietou and Cheti-camp, because the present arrangement of one trip every fortnight is well calculated to destroy the traffic between those points. Does the minister say that the boat carried out its obligations in connection with the changed service?

I am certain that it must have done so because it has been paid the subsidy and unless it had made all the necessary trips, there would be a deduction from the subsidy. The amount
[-ir George Foster.]
of the subsidy was $5,500. In 1914, there were 64 trips, and in 1915, 67. I will look the matter up and let my hon. friend know.

Assuming that the boat goes to Halifax in winter, takes a full cargo from Halifax for persons in North Inverness, and in doing so is unable to take the freight that is waiting at Mul-grave for points along the coast, is that a failure to carry out the contract?

The intent is to serve the country from Pietou from Mul-grave, and from Mulgrave north both ways. If the vessel winters at Halifax, I do not think much fault would be found if on her trip from Halifax to Mulgrave she took a load instead of proceeding empty, provided the people did not lose the service to which they were entitled. They are paid a trip subsidy, and if a trip is omitted they do not get the subsidy for it.

There seems to have been considerable complaint last year on the part of merchants and others along the coast whose expectations of sending out freight by the first trip were disappointed on account of the boat having been filled . at Halifax. However, if these men have not made any representations to the minister, it is their own fault. Practically every year since 1911 I have drawn the attention of the minister to the lightering at at Margaree Harbour. In 1911 the company that had the service undertook to land the freight at their own expense, but this arrangement was discontinued. I would like the minister to take into consideration the question of freight rates. We are paying $1,000,000 for this subsidy, and the very steamers that are being subsidized are charging from five to ten times more for carrying wheat across the AtLantic than was charged formerly. Whereas formerly the rate was generally under 6 cents, and very seldom over 6 cents, during the past season it has

been up to 30, 36, 40, 42, and I am even told 45 cents, though I do not know .myself of any case over 42 cents. If they could make money carrying grain at 5 or 6 cents it seems to me unreasonable that we should pay them the same subsidy as in the past, when they are now charging from 35 to 42 cents. I should like the Minister to consider that point.
I have considered it.

When we pay $1,000,000 subsidy I think we should have some little say as to the freight rates. I know that some increase in rates is legitimate, because insurance on vessels is very much higher than formerly; but other costs, such as coal, wages, etc., are not higher to any great extent. The shipper, however, has to pay five and maybe ten times what he formerly paid for carrying his products across the water before the war. Perhaps the minister could give us some definite information on this matter when the item comes up again.
I shall be prepared to say something definite on that occasion, although I do not know that 1 shall' be able to satisfy my hon, friend.
I think the minister should consider the point raised by my hon. friend from Assiniboia. His point is well taken.
See that the minister satisfies me.

I should not like to undertake that. I am too well acquainted with my hon. friend (Mr. Turriff) to expect the minister to satisfy him. As I may not be in the House . when this item comes up again, I take this opportunity of saying that the point raised by my hon. friend should receive the serious consideration of the minister, and the committee should be given some definite statement upon the matter. I do not know to what extent these vessels carry wheat, but if they are carrying it to any great extent, and are getting 40 to 45 cents for it, they are making plenty of money without a subsidy. That is the only point I wish to make. These ships must be making money if they are carrying wheat to the extent I believe they are. But if they can show that an increase in insurance rates and other costs makes 40 and 45 cents a reasonable price, it is a different matter, and I am open to conviction. My
own opinion is that a great many of the ships are taking advantage of war conditions, and are making a great deal of money; if they are not, let them have the subsidy. But it is up to the Minister of Trade and Commerce to show that they are not making unusual profits before we grant them this $1,000,000.
Mr. PUGSLEY. While these steamers are carrying some grain, they are not carrying a great deal, I am told, because the bulk of Canadian grain to-day is going from United States ports. Portland is crowded with ships carrying Canadian grain to the markets of the Old World, and Canadian ports are getting very little of it. I think the Minister of Trade and Commerce will agree with me in that, and it is a point to which the hon. member for Souris should give attention, because it certainly is not in the interests of Canada that the grain of our great western country should be shipped in such immense quantities through American ports. That is something which many of us have been contending against for a preat many years, and I had hoped that the time had come when it would be no longer possible. In this connection, I was surprised not long ago to see that a railway company whose property this Government has committed Canada to owning to the extent of 49 per cent-the Canadian Northern-had advertised an embargo against western grain via the ports of Fort William and Port Arthur. The embargo did not apply to Duluth or any other American port; so Canadian ports have been rather unfortunate so far as the shipping of grain is concerned. While I am on my feet, I would say to the Minister of Trade and Commerce that I think the time has arrived when this Government should be enabled to announce that the Ministry has taken steps to encourage the building up of a Canadian merchant marine. Nobody knows how long this war is going to last, and the question of the transportation of Canadian products, particularly Canadian food products, to the Mother Country is becoming a most serious one. The public men of Great Britain are giving attention to it. It is stated that neutral vessels are becoming rather shy of taking the risk of being submarined, and are intimating that they can make enough money in other directions, and are thinking of withdrawing their vessels. To-day upwards of one-half of the food supply of Great Britain is carried in neutral vessels. We all know that there has been a great loss in the British mer-

chant marine. During the month of March alone, I believe that some 81 British vessels were sunk by submarines. The war has now been on for upwards of eighteen months. Canada has splendid opportunities for the building of ships on both coasts, and also upon the Great Lakes, where there are two very fine shipyards which have turned out as good vessels as can be built anywhere in the world; and the same remark will apply to the yards on both the Atlantic and Pacific coasts. With a very little expenditure of money, the Government could secure the establishment of shipbuilding plants on both coasts, and the building of ships could be carried on very actively indeed, and they would prove of enormous benefit, not to Canada alone, but to the whole Empire. To-day, after being three months in session, and after having had our attention called to what has been brought up again to-day by the hon. member for Assiniboia and the hon. member for Souris-and we all know that rates have gone up a thousand per cent 'beyond what they were before the war-to me it is a matter for profound regret that up to this late date we have had no intimation that this Government proposes to encourage the building of ships in Canada, and the building up of a Canadian merchant marine.

If we are going to have a debate on this matter, it is not quite fair that a portion should be flung in now, and left to do its deadly work until the answer is forthcoming. My hon. friend should have bottled up his enthusiasm oh this question, which was not so flaming and out-bursting when he was minister in an allpowerful Government in this country. He should have bottled that up and waited until we had the trenches manned on both sides and then we could have had a fair fight. I cannot, however, let my hon. friend's remarks pass without making two or three observations.
In the first place, my hon. friend said that }ie was sorry to know that Portland and other United States ports had been filled up with vessels carrying Canadian wheat whilst St. John and Halifax had been given the go-by. I will inform my hon. friend that St. John and Halifax have had vessels directed to them which have to be diverted owing to the physical impossibility of loading them at either of those two ports, the harbours of St. John and Halifax being filled up to the brim with transport vessels carrying munitions and

supplies fox Great Britain and her Allies, and the precedence that has been necessary for those transports and the congested condition owing to the number of them have been the reasons why more vessels have not come to those ports.
In regard to the taking out of the commandeered grain, I can say to my hon. friend that at least seven vessels were directed to go to St. John and that three or four of them had to be countermanded simply because they could not be filled at that port owing to the congestion on account of this other traffic which is all necessary. The same is true with regard to Halifax. Several vessels directed to Halifax had to be redirected to Portland in order to be filled. I make that state-jnent just to throw a little light upon the subject. My hon. friend went a little out of his way to have a jab at the Government, which he always 'likes to.
It is pleasant. I agree with that.

It is food and nourishment to my hon. friend to have a jab at the Government. He says: Has the Canadian Northern railway, which you have h)ad foisted on to you, which you have taken millions of guarantees in, which is your railway, and which is at your beck and call or ought to be, seeing that you have so much money in it, had the audacity xo make an embargo against Canadian ports while it has not done so against United States ports? Why does a railway make an embargo? Because on the front of it between it and the ports to which it is hauling there is so much congested stuff that it does not dare pile in any more; so it says; Until that is cleared out, I cannot haul in any more. But would it be fair or right to the grain men of the Northwest if, because the railway could not haul any more grain to Canadian ports, they 'should also declare that they would not haul it to American ports where it might find an outlet and an opportunity to get to its ultimate market? I just mention that in order to show my hon. friend that there are two sides to the question. As I have squared this matter up, we will leave the rest of the debate until we all go into it at once. Then my hon. friend here, and my hon. friend there, and the rest Of us will have a talk about it, and I think it would be worth while to talk .ahout a thing like that, a real question which has import in it, which has merit in it, Which has necessity in it,

which is one of the perplexing conditions which the whole world is up against-it would be worth while for this committee, at times when it is devoting itself with a great deal of frivolity to things that might well be left unsaid, if it would put on its thinking cap and devote its powers to the solution of that question. The question of transportation is a lovely theme to talk about, but it is the most difficult and perplexing question in the world to-day, and not much less difficult is the question of the Canadian Government making arrangements for transportation from its own ports to other ports, or undertaking the question of shipbuilding in connection with that same lack of facilities at the present time and that same overplus of demand. Those are very important questions and, when we borne to debate that item early next week, I hope that we shall settle down to a fair discussion of them to see if our combined wisdom can find any way out of this perplexing condition.

I wish I could talk like my hon. friend. I am satisfied, if I could, I could always make an excuse for doing anything. The eloquence of one's talk often makes people forget one's failure to accomplish things. What does the minister say? He says, in beautiful language: Let us get our thinking caps on by and bye; now is not the time, but by and bye let us get our thinking caps on and talk over this important question. If this is an important question, as the minister admits it is, should not the minister lead the way? The Government is in control of this House and of the revenues of this country. This Parliament freely votes to the Government all the money that it wiants. We have already given the Government one-fifth of $250,000,000 to use for war purposes or for purposes which it may deem necessary to advance the interests of this country. We do everything that the Government wants us to do in the way of prosecuting the war successfully, in the way of assisting in upbuilding this country and in the way of improving transportation facilities. Yet, with the attention of- the Government called to the deplorable condition of affairs, a condition which is becoming more deplorable every day, which is becoming dangerous to the Empire and which we ought to confront by doing our part in the assistance of transportation of the food products of Canada'for the people of the Mother Country and in the prosecution of the war, all
the minister can say, after Parliament has been three months in session is: This is a very important question; it is a very difficult question; but we want to get our thinking caps on and we want you gentlemen on the other side of the House to assist us in coming to some conclusion which it would he wise for Canada to come to and which might assist our country and assist the Empire. That is not worthy of this committee; it is not worthy of the people of this country; and I desire to repeat to-day what I said in the opening days of this session, that for its negligence for upvfards of eighteen months since the war broke out, knowing that this .condition of affairs would come about, as the Government must have known, this Government is worthy of the greatest possible blame upon the part of this Parliament land the people of this country, that it has not taken any step of any kind to assist in the transportation of the products of Canada to the Mother Country for the purpose of assisting the Mother Country and the Empire.

My hon. friend does not relish the challenge I threw out that he should get on his thinking cap- not his explosion cap-and when we come to the debate, as we shall, give us his ideas as to practical methods and ways and means by which something may be accomplished. That is what I gave him the invitation for. I wanted him to come down out of the clouds of denunciation of the Government and deploring certain things, and put his very great ability and his very strong mental power into the test to bring out some practical way by which we can help the Mother Country and help ourselves.
. Mr. PUGSLEY: Will the minister promise to- accept my suggestion?

If your suggestion proves to be a good and reasonable and practical one, that is what the Government wants; that is what the Government has long wanted from my hon. friend; but it is what the Government has had very little taste of from him. It consists of denunciation'and of deploring things. What is his practical solution for the transport problem of to-day? I -should like to have his ideas upon it. Will be put on his thinking-cap, -and when we come to this question, as we shall in a few days, will he giv-e us the benefit of his soundest and most practical

judgment as . to how we can bring about these things the lack of which he so much deplores?
If the minister will take advice from this committee, I am sure he will find a large number of members ready with suggestions; but the minister will not ask for suggestions.

I am doing it
now.

Then, I am sure they
will be given.

Would the hon. minister give us an explanation of this item of supervision of subsidized steamship services? The amount is small, but supervision of these services is important. The steamship owners never get tired of taking their money, and I should like the minister to tell us in a word in what the supervision consists.	*
The supervisor is Mr. Tupper, whose salary is $2,500.
One officer for the whole of Canada?

Yes. From the opening of navigation until its closing, Mt. Tupper actually goes on every one of these steamship services on the eastern coast. He takes a trip on the service itself, stops off at the different ports, and makes his observations, and reports to the department. He is also there to make any special report we may wish him to make. He has not time to make the western coast services. He reports as to the condition of the vessel, the life-saving apparatus, the meals, the sanitary conditions, the loading and unloading facilities-everything in connection with the vessel, and makes his recommendations. We draw these recommendations to the attention of the company concerned. I venture to say that the services now, as compared with five years ago, when Mt. Tupper took over this work, are infinitely better in every respect. I have found the owners of vessels1 quite willing to make the necessary small qhanges to improve the life-saving facilities, the sanitary arrangements, and other matters. That is Mr. Tupper's work and he does it very efficiently.
This supervising officer does not deal with the profits that the companies make?

The companies give in their accounts of expenses and receipts, and these are looked over by the supervisor. He was in a bank for some four or five years, and has had experience in that kind of work.
