The Committee resumed at eight o'clock.
Immigration-relief other than-seed grain to settlers on patented and unpatented lands in the provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta-further amount required-Governor General's warrants, $1,550,000.

This is not a new vote;
the money has already been expended. The expenditure was authorized by Governor General's warrant, and in order to legalize it we have to have an appropriation of Parliament.
What was it for?
For relief other than seed grain for the farmers of the West.

What kind of relief
was it?

[DOT] A number of farmers who were left quite destitute as the result of the total loss of crops had to be provisioned during the winter months and well on to the summer, until the time came when the crops were so far advanced that the credit of the farmers was re-established. We had to supply them with provisions and with the general necessities of life, some with fuel, some with clothing. In the southern parts of Alberta and Saskatchewan especially, the farmers were left in very destitute circumstances, and in the emergency, that faced us we had to raise this money under Governor General's warrant.
The money is an advance, is it not?

Yes, we have a lien on
the lands of the farmers to whom assistance was given.

How much was spent
last year, including seed grain and everything?
Mir. ROCHE': For seed grain and relief, $13,362,958. That includes everything- seed grain, relief other than seed grain, fodder.
Do the provincial Governments come in on this?

In 1908 an arrangement was made whereby we lent the money to the Provincial Government, for which they paid us 5 per cent. They advanced the money to the farmers, collected from them and returned it to us as it was collected. This proposition, however, was so large that the Provincial Governments would not have anything to do with it. In the drought-stricken area they did extend relief in the form, of money for road-making. I understand that the Government of Saskatchewan expended in this connection an amount in the neighbourhood of a million and a quarter, but they did not grant relief in the form of seed grain.
Liens were taken on the land; have any of the moneys been repaid?

Some little time ago, somewhere in the neighbourhood of a million and a quarter dollars were returned.
Immigration-relief other than seed grain to settlers on patented and unpatented lands in the provinces of Manitoba and British Columbia, $90,000.

This stands in much the
same position as the other, except that the expenditure was not arranged by Governor General's warrant. We had to grant some relief to the provinces of Manitoba and British Columbia, and as we had no appropriation for these provinces the amount was paid out of the appropriation that had been voted for Saskatchewan and Alberta. On the advice of the Finance Department arid the Auditor General, we are now voting it.

I understand that the
amounts taken for Manitoba and British Columbia, for which there was no vote, came out of the grant to Saskatchewan and Alberta?
Yes.
This is to readjust the account and have it stand against Manitoba and British Columbia in the regular way?

Yes.
Immigration - amounts required for seed grain to settlers on patented and unpatented lands in the provinces of Manitoba and British Columbia, $48,000.

There used to be a well understood rule in the Government that money could not be used for any purpose except that for which it was voted. Has that rule been done away with, and if so, how? This Parliament voted money for
seed grain to settlers in Saskatchewan and Alberta, and apparently without any authority of Parliament part of that money has been diverted to another province. The minister might just as well have taken it out of some of the millions that were voted for public works which were not proceeded with. If he wanted to get this money he should have got it by Governc r General's warrant as for an unforeseen expenditure. I do not know how in the world the Finance Minister could authorize this misappropriation-because that is what it is-of moneys voted by Parliament. A few years ago, such a thing would have been absolutely impossible; it would not have been tolerated by the Minister of Finance, the Minister of Justice, or the Auditor General.

I understand that the
Auditor General was consulted in the matter, and he was quite agreeable so long as it was legalized in this manner. Certain amounts are paid to needy settlers out of our immigration vote every year. This appropriation was to have been legalized on the last day of the last session, but through an oversight it was neglected. The Auditor General and the Finance Department were consulted with regard to this. It was a case of either amending the Act to make it applicable to Manitoba and British Columbia or putting these items in the Estimates, and our advice 'from the Finance Department was that it would he preferable to do it this way.

That means, then, that moneys voted for one purpose can be applied illegally to another purpose upon the understanding that Parliament will pass an Act legalizing what has been done. The Government has no rigfht to assume that Parliament will legalize whatever it does. The ministry should not continually treat members of Parliament as mere automatons who should register whatever the Government may decide upon. It seems to me that the statement of the minister does not improve matters. I do not object to giving this amendment to the settlers in these provinces, but as the expenditure was unforeseen and was not provided for by legislation, the Government should have obtained a Governor General's warrant and afterwards should have asked Parliament to vote the amount. The minister is not unfamiliar with Governor General's Warrants, because we find on page 5 an item for the repurchase of some water-power on

the Winnipeg river. In. 1915, while the war was on, a Governor General's warrant was obtained in this connection for $100,000. The minister could not -have been unfamiliar with the fact that a Governor General's warrant might be applied for to cover cases for which there was no appropriation. I cannot for the moment think that the Government were right in taking the money, which was voted for one purpose, and applying it to another purpose.
It was the same purpose, only in another province.
It was voted to lohn Smith and given to William Brown.
In the same way if the money had been voted for a wharf in Quebec and not used it might be applied to a wharf in Ontario.
That is a technical objection.
In what amounts was the relief provided for given to individuals?
For seed grain there was a maximum of 400 bushels. The relief varied from $1 up to the necessities of the case.

The reason I am asking is that I have heard many complaints during the past year about the amounts of seed grain that were given to farmers having only a quarter section of land to seed. I saw lists showing that farmers with only one quarter section each received from $400 to $500 for seed grain. Of course it may have included fodder for teams to put in the seed. All that money comes as a prior claim to any liens that may be against the land, and I heard some criticism as to the course of the department in granting such large sums in relief under these circumstances.

It may be that the hon. gentleman has been misinformed as to the amount given for seed grain; some of it may have been for relief and some for fodder, because we had to supply many farmers with seed for stock in order to keep their working horses in condition to put the seed in. The maximum amount given to any farmer was 400 bushels, covering all kinds of seed; 2 bushels of wheat to the acre, 3 bushels of oats, and 2i bushels of barley. So that if there were $400 or $500 against a quarter section that might include seed grain, and fodder, and relief as well.

What was represented
to me was that, if $500 or $600 Or $700 had
IMr. Pugsley.}
been advanced by a loan company or any one else, to a farmer with a farm of only moderate quality, of which there would not be 160 acres of land that could be cultivated, the lender found his security to be only a second mortgage, with a first mortgage ahead of it almost as large as the amount he had originally considered it proper to advance on the farmer's property.

The only explanation I can give as to there being $400 or $500 against a quarter section is that I have given. As to our lien on the property having priority, of course that was the condition under which Parliament voted the money, and the Provincial Governments gave us the same security that they had taken under the Provincial Acts of 1908. The loan companies have been protesting at our liens taking priority over their mortgages. That, of course, would not apply to the money advanced by way of relief.
I do not think there was any particular objection on the part of the loan companies to a legitimate advance for seed taking priority.
They objected strongly.

I was not aware of that. I know that in some cases they have expressed the opinion that the seed grain part was all right, as long as it -was legitimately for that purpose; but in many eases settlers obtained grain and did not use it for seed grain but sold it, the value of the grain in these cases ranking as a first mortgage, to the detriment of the holder of the original mortgage.
Could the minister tell us the average amount advanced to farmers in the drought-affected areas last year?

I do not know that we
have struck an average.

I have a ease before me of a man receiving about $1,300 as advances for seed grain and relief, and all he had in crop last year was 100 acres. The complaint here is that this man was given far too much assistance by the Government; in fact it is charged that he was given partial treatment by the distributor of relief.

It is difficult to state the
average in any particular district. We know how many applications for relief were granted, and we know the total amount granted; but we have not the particulars

for any one district. There may have been cases where apparently abnormal quantities of grain were advanced, and of course there must always be some complaints in regard to individual cases.

Does the minister think that the relief granted in the case which my hon. friend from Lethbridge has brought up was fair? Suppose the man had put the hundred acres into wheat, there would have been 150 bushels of seed; and if into oats, 300 bushels. I have had a memorandum prepared by the Water-Powers Branch of the department, which reads:
In the years 1903 and 1904 there was a great deal of activity among parties interested in the development of power along the Winnipeg river for the purpose of supplying the growing market of Winnipeg and district with heat, light and power. Many applications were re-
[Mr. Roche. I
ceived in the Interior Department for waterpower concessions. At that time the value of water-powers and the necessity of their proper regulation and control was not realized and there was no definite policy of water-power1 administration in force. It was the habit of the department to sell lands valuable for waterpower purposes. As there were many applicants to purchase those properties, an auction sale was arranged, lands to be sold on the ten yearly payment plan with interest.
This sale resulted in the purchase of the property in question by the late J. S. Cummins, of Chicago, a partner in the engineering and contracting firm of H. M. Byllesby and Company. The initial payment was made and annual payments continued from time to time. Shortly after the sale was made, the tremendous importance of water-powers was realized, and the department endeavoured to inaugurate an adequate water-power administration. The whole subject was investigated and resulted in the year 1908 in the passing of suitable regulations governing the mode of granting water-power concessions. These regulations provided in short for limited concessions in the form of leases and licenses for twenty-one years, renewable for three further periods, the charging of rental, the control of rates, etc.
The foundation of this method of water-power administration was the retaining by the Crown of its interests in water-powers. This policy could not be carried out if title in fee simple were granted to lands dominating undeveloped water-power sites. It was therefore early realized that the completion of the sale of the lands to Mr. Cummins would controvert the spirit of the water-power regulations. Subsequent surveys and investigations of the water-powers of the Winnipeg river carried on by the department showed that Silver Falls site, which the lands in question dominated, shquld not be developed as a distinct power project, but that these falls should be combined with other falls on the river to make a much larger development, and of course a cheaper development per capital cost, per h.p. Therefore, it was not only necessary from a proper view of administration of water-powers, but also of the best conservation of the natural resources of the river that the department should regain its control over the Silver Falls power site.
The Superintendent of the Dominion WaterPower Branch was authorized to negotiate with Mr. H. M. Byllesby, of Chicago, with a view to the department securing a relinquishment from him of his interest in these properties w1-the negotiations opened there was one payment, the final one, to be made, and a sum approximating $95,842 had already been paid in to the department. An understanding was finally arrived at with Mr. Byllesby, which contemplated his relinquishment of his interest in these properties upon the department refunding to him all moneys paid into the department, and without interest thereon. The essential consideration in this understanding was that a refund should be made immediately. It was therefore necessary to secure the necessary funds by Governor's warrant.
In conclusion it should be pointed out that the department has secured a most satisfactory arrangement in being able to regain its interest in this exceedingly important power site simoly by refunding the actual amounts paid in to the department on the purchase price. It would probably have been reasonable for Mr. Byllesby

to have exacted a considerable sum to cover the value of the water-power site itself. There is no doubt that the financial situation due to present conditions had a great deal to do with the satisfactory nature of the arrangement.
1 Hon. gentlemen will remember that the amendments made to the Dominion Lands Act a few sessions ago provided that in future lands adjacent to water-powers should not be disposed of by sale. As that had been done in this case, negotiations were opened with Bylleshy, who had only one more payment to make, and he relinquished his interest in this property upon the department refunding, without interest, all the money he had paid down.

Such an important principle is involved in this matter that I think the minister ought to bring down all the papers before he asks the committee to pass this amount. As the minister is aware, Governor General's warrants can be issued only for the purpose of repairing or rebuilding some public work which has been destroyed by fire or some other calamity, or for the purpose of meeting some expenditure of an urgent character which could not be foreseen. The words of the statute are very clear. Section 42 of the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act, paragraph (b), says:
If, when Parliament is not in session, any accident happens te any public work or building which requires an immediate outlay for the repair thereof, or any other occasion arises | when any expenditure, not foreseen or provided ' for by Parliament, is urgently and immediately j required for the public good, then upon the re-1 port of the Minister of Finance, etc., etc.
I think we should certainly have a report from the Minister of Finance, and also the papers relating to the negotiations. I think it is important to know when these negotiations began. It certainly does seem to me to be an extraordinary thing that circumstances were such that during recess the Government should have found it necessary to resort to the expedient of obtaining a Governor General's warrant-an expedient which ought to be resorted to only in the rarest possible cases. I think the minister will agree that the papers in this matter ought to be brought down. If these negotiations were carried on in earnest, prior to the last session of Parliament, the Govern-

ment ought to have asked Parliament to make provision for the expenditure involved. These negotiations would not be completed in a week, or a day, or a month, or even six months. of water-powers, was passed some years ago. That is not recent legislation. If the Government contemplated regaining possession of the water-powers which had been disposed of previously, and Parliament had thought there would be any advantage in empowering the Government to do so, it would have made the necessary appropriation. But for the Government to take into its hands this extraordinary and rarely used power, a power which ought to be most sparingly used, of issuing a Governor General's warrant, was a step which requires the very fullest explanation. On March 23, the minister answered a question I asked in regard to the Indian Land Commission in British Columbia. I would like the minister to tell me when this commission was appointed, how long it has been in existence, and if it is still at work.

The hon. gentleman was not here the other evening when we had a discussion on the British Columbia Royal Commission and when the information was all given. It was appointed in the spring of 1913, and it will wind up its labours by the 15th day of May.

I think we can much more conveniently discuss the value of this work after we have received the final report of the commissioners. It is expected that they will report about the 15th of May. The hon. gentleman will remember that the arrangement entered into was that the province of British Columbia should bear one-half of the expense of the commission and the Dominion the other half. The commission entered upon their duties in the spring of 1913. I think these gentlemen have been doing excellent work. It has taken them a very long time, of course. There are eleven or twelve hundred Indian reserves in British Columbia, and each of these had to be visited and the evidence of the Indians taken. The commissioners had to endure a good many hardships in making these trips. The vexed question of Indian lands has been agitating the people of British Columbia for many years, and no proper title to these lands could be given by the Dominion Government because of the reversionary interest claimed by British Columbia. So it was deemed necessary and expedient to have this commission go into the whole question. It was arranged that where reserves were found, upon investigation, to be larger than was necessary for the band, they were to be cut down, but only with the sanction of the Indians; and where reserves were considered to be too small, the British Columbia Government promised to add to them out of other provincial lands. I think this investigation will have the result of putting an end to many longstanding and vexed questions. As to its full value, we shall know better after we have had the final report.

How is it the Public
Works Department is buying stumping powder for this farm at Fredericton? I see the Agricultural Department spent $700 for that purpose last year. There was no election on down there; so how comes it the minister was spending money on stumping?

They were probably
stumping for the location of the building. I would point out that there are two kinds of stumping: the kind that is done in New Brunswick, and the kind that is carried on in western Canada.

This is stumping powder. Does it not strike my hon. friend that as the Minister of Agriculture had spent $700 on stumping powder, this farm could have got along very well without the Minister of

Public Works spending $10 more. While $10 is not a large item, $700 is a large amount to spend on stumping powder.
I do not wish to dispute the statement of my hon. friend, but I think he will find that that $10 item is under the Department of Agriculture.

No, it is under Public
Works according to the Auditor General's Report. I should not expect to find such a small item as $10 for stumping powder among the expenditures of the Agricultural Department. They buy it in $700 worths.
Mr. ROGER'S: Perhaps it was spent on stumping the piggery site.

That is a new theory to put forward. It seems to me absurd to spend $50,000 on that farm when the war is on, and I was very much struck when I saw the item ini the Auditor General's Report under the Department of Agriculture. It shows, as so many other things show, that the ministers, except on rare occasions, do not realize that a war is on, or that there is any difficulty in raising money; they go right along just as if these were peaceful times, and there was no demand for interest upon the war loan, as if we had millions and millions to spend, just as the fancy strikes us. Does not the minister think that $53,000 is an extraordinary amount to spend on this .farm while the war is on? But the minister will not look into it; my words will fall upon deaf ears. Unfortunately the Minister of Agriculture is ill, but some other minister ought to give an. explanation of this item. My hon. friend from Edmonton suggests that as stumping powder was bought, perhaps the Minister of Militia could tell us something about it. Perhaps the item got into this account by mistake. At all events, of this $53,000 that was spent by the Departments of Agriculture and Public Works, upwards of $700 was for stumping powder.

Fredericton, is the capital of New Brunswick; a very important province, and a very important city. Unfortunately, as regards the farm, the district is well wooded, and it was necessary to do a great deal of stumping. My hon. friend spoke of other kinds of stumping a moment ago. I am sure he will realize on reflection that the stumping at the farm is not nearly so expensive as the kind he best understands. As regards the $10 item, the one for which I am responsible, I understand

that this was to 'buy powder with which to clear the ground for the buildings that were erected last year, at a cost of over $10,000.

If stumping powder is used for blasting rock, I can understand that $700 worth be used on this particular farm because I am told it is a very rocky farm and on which nobody with a sincere desire to establish an experimental farm would have thought for a moment of choosing. I am told it was selected because it was near the capital, and because the gentleman who preceded the present member for York, N.B., happened to live in the capital and quite near the experimental farm, and evidently bad a great fancy for the sloping hillside of this particular rocky tract of country which overlooks the St. John river.
I am sure my hon. friend will acknowledge that he was a good judge.

Well, probably he is a better judge now of legal matters than he was when he was a member of this House, of what would make a good experimental farm. I suppose, however, we shall have to let this item go. It is only $53,000 more gone into the sink-hole.

It is only $10.
Dominion public buildings generally, $30,000.

What I have to say has no relation to this item, but perhaps this is as good a time as any to bring to the attention of tJhe committee and of the minister the necessity for making provision for the erection o'f suitable buildings and suitable places for the care of invalid soldiers. We now know some of the conditions that have to be met, and I would certainly urge upon the Government the desirability of making provision, without delay in the 'Supplementary Estimates at this session, for the erection of buildings at suitable points in different parts of the country for the reception of invalided soldiers. The present conditions are not adequate; they are only temporary, and it is a regrettable fact which' stares the country in the face, that there will have to be permanent provision made promptly. I think the Government would be well advised, and I am sure' it would have the support of both sides of the House, if it made provision without any delay. Although we have criticised certain expenditures, desiring to see them cut down
-and we are very glad to see that the minister has agreed not to make certain expenditures at the present time-that is not to say that this matter is not one of immediate urgency and one of the requirements of which should be met adequately and immediately.

Last evening when we
were discussing some of the Estimates of the Department of Public Works, I mentioned that there were some very suitable points in Canada where such buildings as mentioned by my hon., friend should be erected. I specially mentioned Ste. Agathe because it is to-day the rival of Saranac in the Adirondacks. Thh hon. minister mentioned in connection with those hospitals for our returned soldier/s the fact that some wealthy Canadians-and I think he mentioned the name of Mr. Lome McGibbon- had offered their summer residences for use as hospitals. I wish to thank publicly those public spirited Canadians who have done so, and I hope that many others will be found offering their residences for such a noble purpose. I do not, however, believe that the offers made by some of our wealthy Canadians will completely cover the case, as with the large number of soldiers at the front, we may reasonably expect that many will come back crippled and disabled. I would certainly urge upon the minister not to be stingy in this matter of providing accommodation, and as he is not going to spend all the money which has been voted, he might very well be generous in this respect and provide for future possibilities. I certainly endorse the remarks made by [DOT]my hon. friend from Edmonton (Mr. Oliver). We have already seen that some of our soldiers have not been able to find, on their return from the other side, any other place of rest than the streets. I have seen some cases which are simply pitiable, and I call upon my hon. friend, and I make a special [DOT]appeal to his kind heartedness to see that those buildings are erected wherever needed [DOT]in the various sections of Canada.

This is a matter which is engaging the attention of the Government to a very considerable extent. It is true, as my hon. friend from Rouvdlle (Mr. Le-mieux) has stated, that we have had very generous offers from various individuals in the different provinces of Canada to place at the disposal of the Government their summer residences. The one mentioned was offered by Mr. Lome McGibbon, of Ste. Agathe. In addition to this, we have, as

hon, gentlemen will understand, our immigration buildings, which are not in very great use at the present time, at Quebec, Halifax, and other points, [DOT] and they are being turned to this particular use. At the same time the question of more permanent arrangements for our returned, invalided, and disabled soldiers has^ engaged the attention of the Government, and the matter has been turned over to the Military Hospitals Commission-the names of the members of which I am sure are familiar to the members of the House, they being representative individuals from the various provinces of Canada-for a recommendation . on their part after they have had an opportunity of studying the conditions by caring for the returned invalided soldiers, as they are doing at the present time. As soon as their recommendation is before the Government I will see that it is again considered before the Supplementary Estimates come down, with a view, if they make a definite recommendation, of having an amount placed in the Supplementary Estimates ready to meet the conditions.

It is only right to say in regard to this matter of the care of our returned soldiers that on inquiry into the facts it will be found that up to date ample provision has been made for them by the Military Hospitals Commission, and by private generosity. So far as the soldiers who have come back to the military districts in eastern Canada are concerned, I have made the matter a subject of close inquiry, and I do not think that any soldier has been in any difficulty on account of lack of accommodation. There are ample convalescent homes in eastern Canada. We have a very excellent one in our own province. The trouble that has been found in regard to returned convalescent soldiers is to keep them in convalescent homes. Naturally, the desire of the young .Canadian is to return to his relatives, even before he is discharged. The military medical authorities, of course, desire that he should remain in the convalescent home until he is fit to be discharged. While it is true that this Government seems to deal with every problem that comes up by way of commission, and while I cannot sympathize with the feelings of their supporters in their imaginings about the terrible burdens laid upon the Government by the war, I think this Military Hospitals Commission is composed of gentlemen who have performed their duties with great assiduity, and I am bound to

say that, so far as eastern (Canada is con-' cerned, I think that up to date the convalescent soldier has been absolutely well looked after.
IVfr. ROGERS: So far as I have heard and so far as my information goes, I agree with the view expressed by the hon. member (Mr. Macdonald) that the returned soldier has been well looked after. What the hon. gentleman says is true with respect to the provinces of eastern (Canada. But he will understand that conditions in the western provinces are somewhat different. Take, for example, the city of Winnipeg. In that city we have had a very heavy enlistment, and there we have a moving population, including many who, probably, have not the opportunity of having established homes and friends. When the soldiers come back invalided from the war, they all, apparently, like to come back to the point from which they started. It has been suggested to the Military Hospitals Commission that they should make report on this particular aspect of the question of returned soldiers, in order that we may judge what is best to be done. I am sure this House would be very sorry if, regardless of ex-
10 p.m. pense, every returned soldier were not properly cared , for. When we get the report, the. House can depend upon it, the Government will take such action as is necessary to secure every needed comfort for any invalided soldier.
Ottawa public buildings-repairs, including ventilation and lighting, furniture, etc., $415,000.

This is a good deal of
money to spend upon this one service. Does not the minister think that during the war, when there is need of exercising the utmost economy, he could get along very well with half that amount? Ordinary people will not be spending very much this year for new furniture or for making repairs, but will get along as economically as they can. It seems to me that the department might well do with $255,000, thus reducing this vote by $160,000. There is nothing in this vote for new buildings, but the whole amount is for ordinary repairs and furniture.

The department has endeavoured to economize in this vote, but the expenditure has grown by reason of the need to provide for a greatly increased militia staff and for other increases, and for painting, plumbing, and other repair work. The wages paid out of this item in connection with one work amounted to

something like $170,000. In addition, the furniture necessary for all the public buildings is purchased out of this vote. When the disaster overtook us by which the Parliament Buildings were destroyed, a great deal of furniture had to be provided for this building in which Parliament now meets. Practically all of this we shall be able to use because the new Customs building will soon be occupied, and anything purchased for the use of Parliament that will not be required here in the future will find a place in the new Customs building. I am glad to be able to tell my hon. friend that we were so economical and sparing in the expenditure of the vote of last year that when we were overtaken by this disaster we were able to provide all the accommodation that we have in this building without being obliged to ask Parliament for any increased amount. The amount that we have expended in the purchase of desks, chairs, rugs, and so on for the fitting up of this building has been provided out of this vote, and we have a small amount left. My hon. friend will appreciate the fact that we have been very economical. While we are asking for the same amount this year, we will take care that if it is not required it will not be spent.
Rideau Hall, including grounds-improvements, furniture and maintenance, $65,000.

What ds the total amount which will be expended upon the improvements to Rideau Hall? I refer to the large improvements in the facade and the work which was done as part of one operation about a year ago.

We have not the exact
figures; about $175,000, including everything.
Rideau Hall-allowance for fuel and lignt, $17,000.

If we had members who were disposed to criticise along fine Hines, as we had some time ago, it might be suggested that it is difficult to justify the expenditure of $17,000 on fuel and light for this building. But we take a somewhat broader view, and perhaps we should not trouble the minister to go into details. Is this for the dwelling alone, or does it include the out-buildings?

This is the usual vote
that has been passed for many years by this Parliament. It is payable directly to the Governor General for the purposes stated.
The expenditure is not made by the department?
No.

I may recall to my hon. friend the fact that the Royal Society of Canada was founded at Rideau Hall by the late Marquis of Lome, later Duke of Argyle. The society meets sometimes at the Oh ateau , Laurier, sometimes at the Normal School, sometimes at the lOarnegie Library. This society, which is composed of the best intellectual lights in Canada, is subsidized to a small extent by the Dominion Government. It is a national institution, having its meeting place at Ottawa, and it seems to me that the Minister of Public Works, in the reorganization of the public buildings, should find space for the meetings of that society and for its library. I think the hon. minister should be able to find space either in the new Parliament buildings or in one of the adjacent buildings for this purpose. I take this opportunity of expressing also the hope that in the new buildings sufficient space will be provided for the library of Parliament. I have seen the plans and I know that the architects contemplate giving more space to the library, but there are many doubting Thomases in the library; the fear of the librarians is that their wishes may be overlooked. I sincerely hope that my hon. friend will not lose sight of the fact that our library is most precious, and that adequate provision should be made for it in the new buildings.
Ottawa public buildings-telephone service, $42,000.
What is the cost per telephone?

The telephone company charge ordinary people only $25 for one telephone. The Government must have many thousand telephones ; surely the company could make the rate at least as favourable as that which applies to their ordinary patrons.
The charge for a house telephone is $25 and for an office telephone $50. We get a flat rate of $35 a year, so that the difference is in our favour.

We have an excellent telephone service, tout some members who reside in Ottawa, or who spend some time in Ottawa during the recess, find that the telephones are taken from their rooms immediately after the close of the session. If my hon. friend pays $35 a year for each of these telephones it seems to me that the telephones should not be taken away immediately after the session. Those who utilize their rooms during the recess should have the benefit of that service.
The answer to my hon. friend is an evidence of the economy of the present Government. We have a special rate for sessional phones, which are moved out at the close of the session.

I would not regard that as a very strong evidence of economy. The ordinary individual, who is most ignorant of elementary business principles, when he closes his house for five or six months, always has the telephone removed and pays only a pro rata rental.
Not always. My hon. friend does not remove the telephone when he locks up his house.
He would during war time.
Oh, no.

I think this requires some explanation. This is a big item, $42,000 for telephones in the city of Ottawa. It was $39,000 last year, so there is an increase of $3,000 for the present year. How does the minister account for that increase?

This is a matter of increase in the offices requiring phones. The

staff at the present time is very large, owing to war conditions.
That seems to be absolutely true.

But there must be a great many clerks in the Civil (Service who previously used phones who have gone to the war and who were in offices where there has been very little to do since the war broke out. I think that number would counterbalance the increase, which has been in the Militia Department only.
I suppose it is long distance calls.

This is a small increase and it is only an estimated increase. We are not putting in more phones than we need. In fact in my own department I am very sparing in extending the telephone system, and am refusing applications regularly.
Dominion public buildings-rents, $700,000.
I think we should have some explanation of this item. How much of those rente, $700,000, are paid in Ottawa?
What was the rent of buildings in Ottawa four years ago?

I have not the amount
here, but I can get it for my hon. friend.
It was much less.
Yes.
What new public buildings were rented this year?
I have not them indicated in that way.

Has the minister been
in the offices occupied by the Department of Marine and Fisheries in the Rea building?
Yes.

I notice that the rent
paid for the portion of that building occupied by the Department of Marine and Fisheries alone that is the upper stories, is $40,000. Is that not a very heavy rent?

The Navy Department is in that building as well as the Marine and Fisheries Department, and the rent was figured out by the deputy minister on a basis that we have, according to the cost of the building and so on. We endeavour to pay

the same rent according to the value of the property. The rent in this particular instance is 60 cents a foot, which is very cheap compared with other rentals.

I think I saw it given
in the report of the department as 70 cents a foot. That strikes me as high. I remember that I was criticised by you, Mr. Chairman (Mr. Blain), for paying a rental of 41 cents. I think there was a terrible hullabaloo about that. The Minister of Public Works was not here at that time, but these gentlemen who criticised me were pretty level-headed men, and they almost made me believe that I was paying a pretty high rental-they almost made me, they did not quite. But if anybody had suggested that I should jump from 41 .cents up to 70 cents and hope to escape criticism, I would have been astonished. This building is nicely situated, it is true, but there is a large mercantile business being carried on there. The apartments which are rented to the Government are the upper stories, which I do not imagine interfere with the mercantile business at all, and yet the enormous sum of $41,000 or $42,000 is paid for these upper stories. I do not want to be overcritical. I realize that the officials of the department are very careful. They were very careful in my time, and I have no doubt they are so to-day. But the most careful men are liable to be mistaken sometimes, and are liable to be led astray by a minister. I mean nothing personal in that remark. Perhaps the minister could tell us whether he looked into the matter himself, and whether, in his judgment, it is a fair and reasonable amount to pay for offices presided over by one minister.

In the first place, I entirely agree with my hon. friend about the level-headed gentlemen who, questioned his Estimates a few years ago. I quite appreciate the compliment he paid to hon. gentlemen on this side of the House, and I am prepared to fully endorse it. As a result of the care exercised by these hon. gentlemen at that time, a revision of the rents in the city of Ottawa took place, as my hon. friend will Tecollect, and a basis of 6 per cent on the cost was adopted with regard to rentals. That basis has been acted upon, and was acted upon in connection with the offices to which my hon. friend has referred, after the deputy minister had made his own valuation ot the property and office space to be occupied.

How was the valuation arrived at? The Rea Company had a building of three stories, I think, and they were carrying on their business there. They owned the land and the buildings. Another story was put on, or possibly two stories, but the same land would be utilized, and the same support which they had for the buildings would be used for the additional stories. Of course there would have to be an elevator put in. What was estimated as the cost of the new part? Was the land, or a part of the land, taken in? Was the cost of the original building taken into account? Upon a 6 per cent basis, a rental of $42,000 would mean a cost of $700,000.

My deputy informs me that the rental basis is arrived at by a valuation, made by himself, of the property, the land, and of everything connected with the building. Then the part to be occupied is portioned off, and a value placed upon that, based upon its cost. I am informed that the cost of building the additional stories, to which my .hon. friend referred, and of providing new rooms, was $430,000. The rental was based upon a valuation by the deputy minister himself upon the actual cost, the basis being six per cent.

How many new stories
were added?

There were two stories
added to the existing building, and the addition at the north end was all the way up from the ground. The cost, $430,000, did not include the value of the land. Great complaint was made by the people from whom we rented that we would not allow them enough for the space. They wanted 70 cents per cubic foot and we rented at 60 cents. My deputy is satisfied that 60 cents is a reasonable figure.
Dominion public buildings-water, $47,000.

What is the explanation of this?
>
Mr. ROGERS: This item covers water for the buildings all over the Dominion.
Does it include the water purchased by the Government or only the *water supplied from the waterworks?

Only the water supplied
from the waterworks.

Is the Government in a position to tell us what the quality of the Ottawa water is at the present time, or *what steps are being taken to have purer *water supplied in the city? Of course, it

[DOT]is not the Government that supplies this commodity, but the Government is a very large purchaser, and it may have some idea of what is being done in the matter of supplying better water by those from whom [DOT]they purchase.
I understand that the city of Ottawa is bringing in water from Lemieux island through an overland pipe.
We do not use the water for drinking purposes at present; is there [DOT]any chance of being able to do so ?	/
We will probably use the water that is being brought in from Lemieux island, if it is as pure as they say it will be.
How many years will it [DOT]take to finish the work?
They expect to finish the [DOT]work within a year; that is the information we have.
There has been a good deal of discussion about the purification of other things that men drink, but we do not seem to get very far on with the purification of the water which we ought to be drinking.

I should like to call the attention of my hon. friend to the Rea building, not because I want to show the inaccuracy of his statement, but rather to give him an opportunity of correcting it. I find on page 139 of the report of the Minister of Public Works for the year ended March 31, 1915, as follows:
No. 17 0-Ottawa, Ontario-three upper stories of lessors' building, corner Rideau and Sussex streets, 62,907 square feet, at 70 cents per foot.
That is what led me to say 70 cents. The building is occupied by Marine and Fisheries and Naval Service, term expires September 9,	1919, rent $44,034.90 per
annum, lessor paying taxes, heating and elevator service, and lessee paying water. If we multiply the surface area by 70 it gives us the rental exactly; so that is 10 cents a square foot more than the minister seemed to think it was.

My deputy will have it checked up.
Yukon public buildings-rents, repairs, fuel, light, water service and caretakers' salaries, $63,000.

I wish to undo an injustice which I think I did to Mr. Black when the Yukon estimates Were up before. On that occasion I stated that Mr. Black, who is clerk of the Yukon Council and

Public Administrator, had to have his accounts passed by the court, and that as he was frequently appointed judge of the court, his accounts would either have to stand or be passed by himself. I was informed a day or two ago that the accounts of the Public Administrator of the Yukon are audited, not by the judge of the court, but directly from 'Ottawa, an officer going from Ottawa every year for the purpose. I think it only right to make that correction.
